claim: “The movement denoted by the way construction has to be one that consists of a series of stops and starts, rather than being continuous movement.”
evidence_summary: Adele E. Goldberg (1995: 204) states the constraint as motion along a self-created path, either against some external difficulty or deliberate, careful, methodical or winding. Her example (19), from the Wall Street Journal, describes continuous jogging: weaving their way along a street of fractured and fallen houses. CGEL’s own [35v] (p. 689), The track winds its way along the banks of the river, describes continuous, static extension.
finding: A lead, not yet a finding. Attestations of continuous movement (weaving their way along, snaked its way, glided its way) in edited prose would show whether “has to be” overstates the constraint.
inference: Must the movement in the way construction be stop-start?

evidence.passage: §4.3, p. 685. “has to be one that consists of a series of stops and starts”.
evidence.establishes: A lead only. Corpus strings have not been searched.
evidence.note: Local source (working note, unpublished draft or local copy); not online.

evidence.source: Adele E. Goldberg, Constructions: A Construction Grammar Approach to Argument Structure (University of Chicago Press, 1995).
evidence.example: (19), cited from the Wall Street Journal: “weaving their way along a street of fractured and fallen houses”. Verbs such as thread, wend and weave “involve deliberate, careful, methodical, or winding motion”.
evidence.establishes: An analysis that states the constraint as a self-created path. The audit reader reads example (19) as continuous movement.
evidence.locator: Chapter 9, The way construction, p. 204, examples (18)–(19). Page checked on the image by the audit reader.
